text: One photo can produce three different file sizes because each encoder discards the detail your eye tends to skip and then packs what survives, and the three encoders push each step with different intensity. JPEG (1992) splits the image into 8x8 blocks, runs a discrete cosine transform, and rounds off the high-frequency parts. jpegli (Google, 2024) keeps the exact JPEG format but rounds smarter, fitting roughly 25 percent more quality into the same bytes as the older mozjpeg encoder. AVIF borrows AV1's video techniques, including larger blocks and sharper prediction, so it usually wins on bytes per pixel outright.
title: aadhar.sh: thumbnail encoding

text: jpegli writes a normal .jpg that any browser can open, just smaller, because it stays inside the JPEG bitstream; a browser from 1995 still decodes it. AVIF instead needs a modern decoder (Safari 16+, Chrome 85+). That trade between universal-but-larger and modern-but-smaller is why the photo grid ships both formats and lets the browser choose.
title: aadhar.sh: thumbnail encoding

text: AVIF's catch is decode support and encode time. It leans on the AV1 codec, which is slower to encode and only decodes on recent browsers, while jpegli is fast and universal. For that reason the site builds jpegli from source for the universal fallback and uses AVIF as the primary <picture> source: the browser reaches for AVIF first, and anything that cannot decode it falls back to the jpegli .jpg.
title: aadhar.sh: thumbnail encoding

text: Grayscale shots encode much smaller because a color image carries one luma plane (brightness) plus two chroma planes (color). Converting to grayscale deletes both chroma planes, roughly two-thirds of the color information, so the file size falls hard.
title: aadhar.sh: thumbnail encoding

text: Each thumbnail on the site is dual-encoded: an AVIF primary and a jpegli JPEG fallback inside one <picture> element, plus a 400px AVIF tier for phones. The browser loads the smallest format it can decode and never downloads the others.
title: aadhar.sh: thumbnail encoding

text: On one measured 400x266 photo (106,400 pixels), the encoders land at very different sizes against the lossless PNG baseline: baseline JPEG at quality 82, jpegli at quality 82 (roughly half the baseline JPEG), WebP at quality 80, and AVIF at quality 63, with AVIF the smallest of the lossy set. Bytes per pixel is computed by dividing each file's byte size by the pixel count, which makes the encoders directly comparable on a single photo.
title: aadhar.sh: thumbnail encoding

text: Chroma subsampling is a compression technique that stores color information (chroma) at lower spatial resolution than brightness information (luma), exploiting the human visual system's greater sensitivity to brightness detail than to color detail. Common schemes are written as ratios such as 4:4:4 (no subsampling), 4:2:2 (chroma sampled at half horizontal resolution), and 4:2:0 (chroma sampled at half resolution both horizontally and vertically). The savings come because the eye notices reduced color resolution far less than reduced brightness resolution.
title: Chroma subsampling (Wikipedia)

text: AVIF (AV1 Image File Format) is an image format that stores images or image sequences compressed with the AV1 video codec inside the ISOBMFF container. Because it reuses AV1's intra-frame coding tools, it generally achieves smaller files than JPEG and WebP at comparable quality, and it supports features such as high dynamic range, wide color gamut, alpha transparency, and both lossy and lossless compression. Browser support arrived around 2020 in Chrome and 2022 in Safari.
title: AVIF (Wikipedia)

text: JPEG is a widely used lossy compression method for digital images, standardized in 1992, that works by transforming 8x8 pixel blocks with a discrete cosine transform and then quantizing the resulting frequency coefficients. The degree of quantization sets a tunable tradeoff between file size and image quality, and the format commonly applies chroma subsampling to reduce color data. Its near-universal decoder support is the main reason it remains a default web image format decades later.
title: JPEG (Wikipedia)
